{"durationSeconds":574.403,"fileName":"voice_en_105.wav","id":"666A8A59","language":"en-ZA","name":"voice_en_105","segments":[["For a while, the front doors of Galveston opened onto empty air.",0,4.5],["Beneath the houses stood forests of wooden supports.",4.5,8.22],["Above the muddy ground, narrow walkways led people home.",8.22,12.24],["This was not the storm itself.",12.24,15.12],["This was the rebuilding, and it began with an extraordinary question.",15.12,20.28],["How do you save a city when the ground beneath it is too low.",20.28,24.72],["At the turn of the 20th century, Galveston was one of the busiest ports in the American South, cotton moved through its docks, trains brought goods and visitors, ships connected Texas to the wider world.",24.96,38.7],["But Galveston had a weakness that could not be seen on a ledger.",38.7,42.72],["The city stood on a long, low barrier island off the Texas coast.",42.72,47.4],["The highest natural ground on the island was estimated to be less than 9 feet above sea level.",47.4,53.46],["The sea was part of its prosperity, but it was also close enough to become a threat.",53.46,58.62],["In June 1900.",58.74,61.56],["The census counted almost 38,000 people in the city.",61.56,64.56],["Families lived in wooden houses.",64.56,67.2],["Children walk to school.",67.2,69.18],["shopkeepers opened their doors.",69.18,70.8],["For most of them, September 8th began like another day on the Gulf Coast.",70.8,75.54],["Days earlier, a tropical storm had crossed Cuba.",75.78,79.8],["It strengthened as it moved across the Gulf.",79.8,82.32],["At the time, there were no weather satellites, no radar maps on a phone, and no way for forecasters to follow a hurricane over open water with anything like modern precision.",82.32,93],["Reports came from scattered observations, ships, and telegraph stations.",93,98.04],["A storm warning flag was raised in Galveston on September 7th, the danger was not entirely unknown.",98.04,105.3],["But many residents did not expect the catastrophe that was approaching.",105.3,109.38],["Some had experienced earlier storms, and believed their city could withstand another.",109.38,114.42],["Isaac Klein, the local weather bureau official watched conditions change.",114.42,119.46],["The next day, the sea was rising, the wind was strengthening, and the information reaching the public could not show the full scale of what was coming.",119.46,128.34],["On the morning of September 8, water began creeping into the streets.",128.46,133.02],["Then the Gulf pushed farther inland.",133.02,135.9],["By afternoon, people who had expected bad weather were confronting something far worse.",135.9,141.3],["The water was not simply rain collecting in low places. The hurricane drove a massive surge across the island.",141.3,148.56],["The storm surge was later estimated at nearly 16 feet.",148.56,153.72],["Waves carried timbers, pieces of houses, and everything else they could tear loose.",153.72,158.16],["As debris struck buildings, some walls gave way.",158.16,161.76],["Other structures were lifted from their foundations, people climbed to upper floors and gathered in stronger buildings.",161.76,169.08],["Families took in neighbours.",169.08,170.7],["One building that survived was the Gresham family's stone house, known today as Bishop's Palace.",170.7,177.18],["According to accounts of survivors, more than 200 residents found refuge there.",177.18,182.04],["Yet height offered little certainty, as water and wreckage moved through the city.",182.04,186.9],["At the Weather Bureau, the wind gauge recorded gusts of roughly 100 miles an hour before it blew away.",186.9,193.74],["Conditions grew more violent into the evening.",193.74,196.56],["Darkness made it harder to see where the water ended or what was coming toward a house.",196.56,201.9],["Klein and his family struggled to survive.",201.9,204.84],["His wife died in the storm.",204.84,207.06],["Their loss was one among thousands across Galveston.",207.06,211.14],["And many families would never be whole again.",211.14,213.72],["Near midnight, the wind and water finally began to subside.",213.72,218.16],["What daylight revealed was a city transformed, streets were buried beneath wreckage.",218.16,224.34],["Houses had disappeared or been torn apart.",224.34,227.22],["Survivors searched for relatives among unfamiliar piles of broken timber.",227.22,231.9],["The death toll could never be counted with complete certainty.",231.9,235.38],["At least 6000 people died.",235.38,238.26],["Some estimates are considerably higher, and the storm remains the deadliest weather related natural disaster in United States history.",238.26,246.3],["The city faced an immediate task as terrible as the storm itself, caring for the living and finding the dead.",246.3,253.62],["Temporary morgues were established.",253.62,255.78],["As the scale of the losses became clear, recovery workers struggled with more bodies than the city could handle.",255.78,262.26],["Aid came from outside, but the future was uncertain.",262.26,265.74],["Galveston could rebuild its homes and businesses.",265.74,269.22],["Yet if another hurricane drove water over the island, the same low ground would be waiting beneath them. Rebuilding also meant living with uncertainty.",269.22,278.04],["A replacement house could be swept away by a future surge.",278.04,281.58],["Businesses needed a functioning port, families needed homes, and the island needed a way to face the water that surrounded it.",281.58,289.02],["The question was no longer simply how to restore the city.",289.02,292.56],["It was how to give it a better chance next time.",292.56,295.32],["A board of engineers proposed two connected defences.",295.32,298.98],["First came a seawall along the Gulf side, a massive barrier designed to meet the waves before they reached the streets, but a wall alone would leave a problem behind it.",298.98,309.18],["Much of the city still lay close to sea level.",309.18,312.06],["The second part of the plan was almost harder to imagine.",312.06,315.36],["They would raise the ground.",315.36,317.22],["And before the ground could rise, buildings standing on it would have to rise too.",317.22,322.68],["Work on the 1st section of the seawall began in 1902.",322.68,326.82],["By 1904, a concrete barrier about 3.3 miles long stood along the Gulf.",326.82,333.18],["Its top rose 17 feet above mean low water.",333.18,337.08],["Later extensions would carry the wall farther along the coast.",337.08,340.56],["While the seawall was being built, the grade raising project turned neighbourhoods into construction sites behind it, the work moved from section to section.",340.56,349.98],["Crews lifted buildings on hand operated screwjacks and supported them on temporary timbers, about 2,000 buildings were raised, according to the American society of civil engineers.",349.98,361.5],["That number tells only part of the story.",361.5,364.92],["A building could not simply be set aside while a new foundation was prepared.",364.92,368.76],["It had to remain supported as crews worked below and around it, and every raised house stood among streets and services that needed to connect at a new level. Water pipes, fire hydrants, and street car tracks also had to be dealt with as the level of the ground changed.",368.76,384.84],["This was not a model on an engineer's desk.",384.84,388.08],["It was a living city, full of structures that had to be kept in place while the land around them was remade.",388.08,394.26],["To bring in the material, a canal was cut through part of Galveston, dredges collected sand and carried it through the canal.",394.26,401.52],["Workers then pumped Phil into the areas being raised, including spaces beneath the lifted buildings.",401.52,407.64],["The amount varied from place to place.",407.64,409.8],["The aim was not to lift every street to exactly the same height, but to create a higher sloping grade behind the seawall.",409.8,417.54],["What looked like chaos had a purpose.",417.54,419.82],["Sand gradually became the new ground on which the city would stand.",419.82,424.08],["Once an area was filled to its new grade, foundations could be finished beneath the structures.",424.08,430.2],["Work could then move onto another section.",430.2,432],["The change was gradual.",432,434.04],["Not a single dramatic lift of the entire island.",434.04,436.68],["Some residents continued living in their houses during the work.",436.68,440.28],["To get around, they used makeshift boardwalks raised above the muddy fill. Imagine stepping out of a front door onto a narrow wooden path while crews reshaped the ground below.",440.28,451.08],["The transformation also came at a cost.",451.08,453.78],["Taxpayers helped finance the work, and property owners had to pay for lifting their buildings, as streets and sidewalks disappeared beneath Phil, residents face the expense of replacing them too.",453.78,465.12],["The engineering solution was remarkable, but rebuilding placed real burdens on the people who remained.",465.12,471.48],["One of the most striking challenges was St. Patrick's Church, the building weighed an estimated 3000 tons.",471.48,478.86],["According to the Galveston and Texas History Centre, workers used 700 jacks to raise it 5 feet, a heavy masonry church, moved upward not by a single enormous machine, but by the patient coordination of many smaller lifts.",478.86,493.74],["The main work continued for years.",493.74,496.14],["Temporary supports disappeared beneath new foundations.",496.14,499.8],["The temporary canal was filled back in, streets were rebuilt.",499.8,504.12],["Little by little, the strange city of boardwalks and raised houses gave way to a more familiar one.",504.12,510.48],["Then, another hurricane put the defences to the test.",510.48,514.2],["In 1915, a powerful storm struck the region.",514.2,518.22],["Galveston suffered damage, but the loss of life in the city was far lower than in 1900.",518.22,523.74],["The seawall and raised ground had become part of a broader response to a danger the city now understood much better.",523.74,530.52],["That did not make Galveston invulnerable. Hurricanes continued to threaten the island, and in 2008, Hurricane Ike brought a major surge to the Texas coast.",530.52,540.54],["No wall can erase the sea, or guarantee that every future storm will be survived without loss.",540.54,546.66],["But the people of Galveston had done something extraordinary.",546.66,550.2],["After a disaster that destroyed thousands of lives.",550.2,553.5],["They chose not only to rebuild their city, they changed the ground beneath it.",553.5,558.18],["For years, home stood above muddy streets, while workers brought in the sand that would make a different Water pipes, fire hydrants, and street car tracks also had to be dealt with as the level of the ground changed.",368.76,384.78],["This was not a model on an engineer's desk.",384.78,388.08],["It was a living city, full of structures that had to be kept in place while the land around them was remade.",388.08,394.26],["To bring in the material, a canal was cut through part of Galveston, dredges collected sand and carried it through the canal.",394.26,401.52],["Workers then pumped Phil into the areas being raised, including spaces beneath the lifted buildings.",401.52,407.7],["The amount varied from place to place.",407.7,409.8],["The aim was not to lift every street to exactly the same height, but to create a higher sloping grade behind the seawall.",409.8,417.54],["What looked like chaos had a purpose.",417.54,419.82],["Sand gradually became the new ground on which the city would stand.",419.82,424.08],["Once an area was filled to its new grade, foundations could be finished beneath the structures.",424.08,430.2],["Work could then move onto another section.",430.2,432],["The change was gradual, not a single dramatic lift of the entire island.",432,436.68],["Some residents continued living in their houses during the work.",436.68,440.28],["To get around, they used makeshift boardwalks raised above the muddy fill.
